title: Who looks after our public spaces?
label: 10 November 2026 · Public spaces
summary: The committee explored how clean, safe public spaces affect people’s pride, wellbeing and willingness to visit or invest in an area. Witnesses described effective partnerships between councils, businesses and community groups, but said councils often lack the money, staff, data and powers to maintain spaces and enforce rules. They proposed clearer responsibility across boundaries, better coordination of street works and waste collection, practical use of technology, education and long-term funding. They disagreed on whether enforcement fines should be uniform nationally or tailored locally, and said it remains uncertain whether public spaces have actually deteriorated or people’s expectations have risen.

chapters.title: Why well-kept places matter
chapters.takeaway: Clean, cared-for streets can encourage pride, investment and good behaviour, while neglect can put people off.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What difference does it make when public spaces are well maintained?

turns.speaker: Councillor Carl Cashman
turns.text: People are more likely to visit, invest in and take pride in a place that is looked after. Liverpool ONE shows what can happen when a developer and the council keep working together after a site is built: it has become a place people want to shop, visit and spend money.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: A neglected street sends a message that nobody is responsible for it. That can affect how people behave and make employers, workers and investors less keen to be there. I know of potential tenants who turned away from a fine refurbished building because the street outside felt uncared for.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Litter, abandoned phone boxes, road signs left around and badly managed works all add to that impression. Better-off areas can also find it easier to get problems fixed because residents and businesses often know how to navigate the systems. That creates an unfair difference between neighbourhoods.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: When I worked in Windsor, businesses left rubbish bags out because they assumed the council would clear them. Residents copied them, and eventually someone drove up and added their own bags. People had come to see the street as a free disposal point.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: We spoke to businesses, checked waste arrangements, and took action against those who kept breaking the rules. The visible presence and conversations on the street mattered as much as penalties. People often change their behaviour when they understand what they should do and know someone is paying attention.

turns.speaker: Simon Mantle
turns.text: You need to listen to the people who live and work in an area, not assume you already know how it should be used. A clean, well-planned space supports local shops and visitors. And, as others have said, behaviour tends to follow what people see around them.

turns.speaker: Councillor Carl Cashman
turns.text: Councils want to look after public spaces, but their budgets are under pressure from services such as adult social care and support for children with special educational needs. Councils need enough funding to do the work; private partners and BIDs can help, but shouldn't have to make up for everything councils can't afford.

chapters.title: Working across organisations
chapters.takeaway: Partnerships can solve local problems, but they need clear responsibilities, shared information and sustained funding.

turns.speaker: Lord Cameron of Dillington
turns.text: How can public bodies, businesses and others work together, and what gets in the way?

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: In rural Rushcliffe, fly-tipping complaints were being dealt with by clearing the rubbish, but the people responsible kept doing it. We investigated before the council cleaned up, gathered evidence and followed up with offenders. Complaints fell by 60% in the first year, but then some offenders simply moved across the border.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: Working with neighbouring councils helped because the same offenders were operating in several areas. Councils should also be able to check what a contracted company is doing, including officers’ camera footage and case records. But investigators need suitable access to information to identify offenders and connect cases.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: BIDs, major employers and large property owners can work productively with councils. But they often spend their own money on basic cleaning rather than the events and improvements they would prefer to fund. That helps in some places, but it can't replace council services everywhere.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Some problems need clearer rules. Phone boxes can be expensive and slow for councils to remove, even when they're left in poor condition. Charging the companies responsible could encourage them to deal with them. Lane rental charges can also make utility companies pay for occupying roads, and the money could help with street cleaning.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Commercial rubbish collection can involve many companies making separate trips, and waste left behind then falls to councils to clear. New York has limited which companies can collect commercial waste in each area. We could consider similar ways to organise the service, alongside better use of bins and stronger penalties for poor road repairs.

turns.speaker: Councillor Carl Cashman
turns.text: Councils are well placed to bring residents, businesses and other organisations together because they know their areas. But they need the staff and time to do it. Liverpool ONE also shows why a new building or investment isn't enough: someone needs to keep caring for the place afterwards.

turns.speaker: Councillor Carl Cashman
turns.text: Utility companies should be held responsible when their work damages or disrupts public spaces. New powers such as lane rental only help if councils have the resources to use them. Businesses often want cleaner streets too, because that brings customers and makes an area more attractive.

turns.speaker: Simon Mantle
turns.text: We try to reduce the number of separate waste collections by getting businesses to use the same provider and coordinating collection times with the council. We also work with charities to support people experiencing homelessness, with the aim of building trust and helping them find routes off the street, not simply moving them on.

turns.speaker: Simon Mantle
turns.text: In Kensington, residents raised concerns about noisy and speeding cars. The council, police and local partners used mobile cameras to monitor the area; within 11 days, 130 fines had been issued and vehicles had been seized. It shows how partners and technology can help where police can't be present all the time.

chapters.title: Who takes responsibility?
chapters.takeaway: Busy places with many owners and agencies need one clear lead, while local areas need powers to address problems that cross boundaries.

turns.speaker: Lord Bassam of Brighton
turns.text: Brighton station is a mess, but the area involves the council, rail and bus operators, police, food outlets and waste companies. Who should take responsibility when so many organisations use the same space?

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: Birmingham New Street station had similar problems. The council, British Transport Police and Network Rail worked together, and Network Rail took a leading role. Funding allowed officers to tackle litter and anti-social behaviour. Within months, the station and surrounding area had improved considerably.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: The work also involved serious risks, including finding people carrying weapons and responding to overdoses. It needed police support and proper funding; visible officers on the ground were essential.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Some problems are made harder because local authorities don't have the same powers as large cities such as New York. Giving local areas more authority—with safeguards—could let them respond to local needs, for example by coordinating roadworks or organising rubbish collection.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Different companies dug up the same streets several times to install separate fibre networks. A 'dig once' approach would let them share one trench. But we also need councils to benefit when local business activity grows, rather than having extra income taken away through national funding adjustments.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Boundaries can move a problem rather than solve it. After action against noisy cars in one part of London, residents saw the problem in another. Multiple borough and police boundaries can make it hard to organise a response across a city.

turns.speaker: Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe
turns.text: Could you provide examples of how 'dig once' could be made enforceable, and explain what different arrangements between town, district and county councils mean for local services?

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon
turns.text: Are councils able to use their enforcement powers effectively, and do they have the people and systems to do it?

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: The rules are mostly there, but there's a gap: someone who breaks a public spaces protection order can refuse to give an authorised officer their details and walk away. Littering rules do require people to give their name and address. Extending a similar requirement to these cases would help officers follow up.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: Many councils also lack effective systems to issue and track penalties. Officers may have to write them down and enter the details later, then manage reminders, payments, complaints and possible court cases. Those steps take time, and some old systems don't support them well.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Businesses often want to see uniformed police, but many different teams can be involved: police, council officers, BID patrols, property owners and transport police. That can leave gaps and confusion about who is responsible. Councils are effective at enforcing parking rules; it raises the question of why other street problems don't get the same attention.

chapters.title: Enforcement, education and fairness
chapters.takeaway: Consistent, well-supported enforcement can help, but penalties must be fair and prevention and education matter too.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: Parking enforcement is required and usually has proper technology behind it. Environmental enforcement is optional for councils, so some lack staff and suitable systems. The same officers can do both kinds of work, and some councils already use them for both.

turns.speaker: Councillor Carl Cashman
turns.text: More penalties aren't the answer on their own. Councils need enough people on the street to make rules real and prevent repeat offences. I also don't think every area needs the same fine: local authorities should be able to set penalties that suit local circumstances.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: Whatever the penalty, councils need a fair process: people should be able to challenge a notice, explain genuine hardship and have their case reviewed. A large fine can be impossible for someone who can't afford basic necessities.

turns.speaker: Simon Mantle
turns.text: Technology can help cover more ground and make people feel that a space is being watched, but it can't replace good management or people working with the community. Businesses sometimes wash the pavement outside their premises because its condition matters to their success.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon
turns.text: Schools can help children understand the effects of litter. In my area, pupils go out to pick it up. Could councils do more to encourage that kind of work?

turns.speaker: Baroness Janke
turns.text: Community groups and schools can also turn neglected land into gardens, grow food and teach children about wildlife. These projects give people a reason to value and care for their neighbourhood.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: BIDs and local groups already work with schools, employees and volunteers on planting and community activities. But we often have to spend money on basic cleaning instead. We should also look at better equipment and methods for cleaning streets, rather than assuming the old approach is the only option.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: Our teams visit schools, run litter picks and organise competitions. We reached more than 10,000 children in 2025, but we often need councils to help us get access to schools.

turns.speaker: Simon Mantle
turns.text: We run outdoor learning for local schoolchildren and work with the London Wildlife Trust to teach about planting and the environment. When children help make and care for a space, they can develop a lasting sense of pride in it.

chapters.title: Paying for long-term care
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses called for stable funding and clearer local powers, while disagreeing over how much enforcement should be standardised.

turns.speaker: Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe
turns.text: What is the best way to pay for maintenance and enforcement, and how can long-term care be built into development agreements?

turns.speaker: Simon Mantle
turns.text: The Community Infrastructure Levy could help pay for public spaces. Developers and property owners can invest, but ongoing care needs a long-term commitment, not just money for construction. Our work on sites we develop includes continuing stewardship.

turns.speaker: Councillor Carl Cashman
turns.text: Local BIDs could help improve high streets beyond city centres. Prescot, for example, had a major town-centre renewal, including improved shopfronts. But councils still need funding to maintain spaces across whole cities, not just busy commercial areas.

turns.speaker: Councillor Carl Cashman
turns.text: Councils often get blamed when work by a utility company disrupts a park or street, even though they may not be responsible for it. The companies and businesses that cause waste or disruption should also be held accountable, and councils need the resources to enforce that.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Local taxes should help pay for the streets and public spaces people use every day. Councils should also keep more of the extra income generated when an area grows, so they have a reason and the means to invest in it.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Charges on companies that leave phone boxes in disrepair or occupy roads could both discourage the problem and help pay for its costs. Visitor charges could also support the places visitors use. Better coordination across council boundaries could reduce duplicated services and make budgets go further.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: Councils choose how enforcement is paid for. Some pay for it directly; others use penalties to cover the service. Enforcement shouldn't be about raising money or hitting a target number of fines. It should be about improving behaviour, and the company delivering it shouldn't decide the penalty amount.

turns.speaker: Lord Bassam of Brighton
turns.text: What recommendations would make the biggest difference?

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: Make environmental enforcement more consistent with parking enforcement, and consider having the same officers do both. A shared process for issuing and following up penalties would help. A database that councils can use together would also help them trace waste offenders who move between areas.

turns.speaker: John Dunne
turns.text: And close the gap that lets people walk away from officers after breaking a public spaces protection order without giving their details. That would make it easier to follow up cases.

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Use changes to the law to make roadworks easier to coordinate, give local authorities better ways to manage commercial rubbish collection, and charge companies for problems such as roadworks that overrun or phone boxes left in poor condition. These steps needn't all require new public spending.

turns.speaker: Councillor Carl Cashman
turns.text: I support shared processes and cooperation across boundaries, but not necessarily one fine for the whole country. Different places may need different penalties. Real devolution means giving power and funding to the lowest practical level, while still finding ways to coordinate across larger areas.

turns.speaker: Councillor Carl Cashman
turns.text: The basic point is that councils are willing to work with businesses and use their powers, but without enough funding they can't maintain and enforce standards across their areas.

turns.speaker: Simon Mantle
turns.text: Make it easier to combine public and private funding, while ensuring private investment adds to a properly funded basic public service. And judge projects by whether they improve safety, access, wellbeing and local business, not simply by whether a new square or refurbished street has been delivered.

turns.speaker: Baroness Andrews
turns.text: We heard clear examples of what can work, but do we know whether public spaces have actually got worse over the past five or ten years? Could research help explain why people feel they have?

turns.speaker: Alexander Jan
turns.text: Accounts from a century ago also described London as dirty, so it may not be a new problem. I think some places have improved, but people's expectations have risen too. The quality of homes and cars has changed much more than the public spaces around them, so streets can feel disappointing by comparison.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The committee would welcome further examples, including from smaller councils, and ideas on clarifying responsibilities, reducing costs and keeping public spaces well maintained over time.
